messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ingrid is a 43-year-old chef who nearly died two years ago from sepsis that set in after she tasted a batch of raw oysters at the restaurant where she had worked for a decade. Within hours she was in the ICU with a fever of 105, her organs beginning to fail. She remembers the sensation of her own blood turning against her—the violent chills, the way her skin felt like it was on fire, the terror that she would never leave that bed. She spent three weeks in hospital and another month recovering at home, but the body she came back to did not feel like her own.

What frightened her most was that her body kept acting as if the danger had not passed. Even now, a sudden rise in her heart rate from climbing stairs or a flush of warmth in the kitchen sends her into a full-blown flashback: she is back in the hospital bed, the beeping monitors, the metallic taste of fluid on her tongue, the grief of believing she would never feel normal again. The memory comes with all her senses at once—the smell of antiseptic, the bright overhead light—and it is so extreme that sometimes she has trouble believing it actually happened to her. When she recalls the event, the grief washes over her, raw and overwhelming.

Ingrid came to believe that her body is permanently damaged, that it will always be her enemy, and that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again. These beliefs drive everything else. Because she is certain her body cannot be trusted, she scans for any physical sensation that might signal disaster—a racing pulse, a twinge in her chest—and this hypervigilance triggers more intrusive memories. The memory, in turn, confirms that her body is unsafe, tightening the loop. To cope, she has learned to numb her feelings: she stays up until two or three in the morning, delaying sleep because the dark silence leaves room for the flashbacks. She also avoids anything that might make her feel happy or hopeful, because hope feels like an invitation for her body to betray her again.

Her occupation as a chef has become a minefield. She can no longer taste raw shellfish—the smell alone can bring the full sensory reliving—so she delegates that task, making excuses to her sous chef. The heat of the sauté station, the steam from the dishwasher, even the press of her chef's coat against her skin when she is sweating can set off her body reacting before her mind has even registered a threat. She cannot relax even when she knows she is in a safe place, because safety does not feel real. Over the weeks, the numbing strategies have backfired: the more she avoids positive events, the more convinced she becomes that she has lost the capacity for joy, reinforcing her belief that she is permanently broken. Her partner has noticed her pulling away, and she has stopped going to family dinners.

The cumulative effect is exhaustion. Her delay sleep means she is chronically tired, which only makes her more reactive to perceived threats, and the reactive body sensations feed the flashbacks again. She finally sought help when, one evening in the walk-in cooler, a sudden temperature drop made her gasp and she fell to her knees, certain she was having another medical emergency. She is afraid that she will never trust her body again, but she is even more afraid that if she does not stop the cycle, she will lose her job and her relationship—everything she fought to return to.
